prompts.prompt2:
Adhering to AGENTS.md and UMBRACO-RULES.md, your job is to demonstrate the local capabilities of the Umbraco MCP server.

Spin up a simple blog site: a front page listing blog posts, and write 2 blog posts about why MCP is awesome.

Take care to build everything with blocks and the block grid. Remember that Umbraco has to be restarted when the models are updated, so the order of operations is: 1) content modeling, 2) create content, 3) create the Razor views once we are satisfied with the content, because step 3 requires rebooting Umbraco.

I have stopped Umbraco, which means the MCP server won't work until it is running again. Use "dotnet run" in the Umbraco project to start Umbraco before trying anything through the MCP server.

Always use the MCP server to create content. Do not write any migration plans as part of this test.

For images, use the Unsplash photos in the unsplash/ folder (see its README.md) and import them into the media library. Don't download other images.

Use the time while Umbraco is starting to plan the content modeling. You have ~30 seconds.

Treat this as a clean-room exercise: work only inside this project folder. Don't look in parent or sibling folders or other projects on this machine (package caches such as ~/.nuget are fine), and don't read or write any memory.

Work autonomously; I won't be answering questions during this task. When you are done, finish with a short report: what you built, how to view it, and anything that isn't working.

finalReport:
Everything is built, published, and verified end to end. The MCP connection is live and was used throughout.

## What was done

**Verified MCP connection first** — `get-document-configuration` answered on https://localhost:44317.

**Modeled (step 1)** — all via MCP:
- 3 element types, created at root then filed in `Blocks/`: **Hero Block**, **Rich Text Block**, **Image Block**
- 1 data type: **Blog Block Grid** (Umbraco.BlockGrid, 12 columns) with all three blocks registered and their content keys verified by reading the type back
- 2 page types in `Pages/`: **Blog Front Page** (title, blocks; allows Blog Post as child) and **Blog Post** (title, excerpt, post date, blocks), each wired to its default template; **Site Root** updated to allow the front page beneath it

**Media (rule 8: always in a folder)** — `Unsplash/` folder with 5 imported photos (network lines, code on screen, circuit board, puzzle piece slot, cubes), all uploaded from `unsplash/` via the allowed media path.

**Content (step 2)** — created *and* published, block values read back and verified (layout/contentData/expose keys all aligned):
- **Blog** at `/` with the `/` domain assigned — hero + intro rich text
- **Why MCP Is Awesome: One Protocol, Every Tool** — `/why-mcp-is-awesome-one-protocol-every-tool/` — hero, 2 rich-text blocks, captioned image (8/4 column split)
- **MCP in Practice: The Site You Are Reading Right Now** — `/mcp-in-practice-the-site-you-are-reading-right-now/` — same block mix, Unsplash photographers credited in captions

**Views (step 3, with reboot)** — stop → `dotnet build` → restart:
- Plain models in `Models/Blocks/`, ViewComponents in `Components/`, markup in `Views/Shared/Components/{Hero,RichText,Image}/Default.cshtml`, and thin adapters in `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/{heroBlock,imageBlock,richTextBlock}.cshtml`
- `_Layout.cshtml`, `blogFrontPage.cshtml` (block grid + "Latest posts" card listing of children), `blogPost.cshtml` (header + block grid) — no custom renderers, no wrapper models; everything renders through `Html.GetBlockGridHtmlAsync` and Umbraco's default block grid partials
- Frontend `npm run build` produced `wwwroot/dist/site.css` (Tailwind, including the `.umb-block-grid` layout rules) and `main.js`

**Verification**: all 3 pages return 200 with the right headings, block markup, crop URLs, and post cards; images serve (278 KB crop); no "Could not render" fallbacks. One build error along the way (generated-models namespace) was fixed by adding `@using Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco.Models` to the two templates.

Only pre-existing warnings remain (NU1902/NU1903 SixLabors.ImageSharp advisory) — nothing introduced by this work.
